He notes how slavery looks different to each judge. To the moralist it is the sum of all villainies, to the reformer the negation of right, to the economist a system of labor. To the historian it is a step from killing captives to living by the sweat of other men's faces. Noting that the Panama Canal's opening marks four hundred years since Black slavery's introduction, Hershaw turns to the debt-labor system that succeeded it. The paper is a sharp, early study of unfreedom after emancipation.
31640-crestlands-a-centennial-story-of-c:
Mary Addams Bayne's novel Crestlands, a centennial story of Cane Ridge, was published at Cincinnati by the Standard Publishing Company, with copyright in 1907, and illustrated by O. A. Stemler. Its frontispiece shows Abner gently checking his mare and sitting to watch a woman. The book is set at Cane Ridge, a place of meeting houses and revivals.

Its chapters open with the coming of the schoolmaster, then getting to work, and the Cane Ridge meeting house. A great revival follows later in the book. Bayne's novel tells a centennial story of a Kentucky community, its school, its church, and its people across a changing time.
31758-call-him-savage:
John Pollard's short story was printed in Amazing Stories in March 1954. It is told by a writer working on a tale of a Sioux rising against a white settlement at the fork of the Platte. As he writes of Chief Spotted Horse and an attack set for dawn, his wife interrupts him, and the frontier story keeps breaking into his home life.

The humor comes from that split: the narrator's imagined war whoops and heroic speeches sit beside midnight talk, a cold, and a chapter still unfinished. Readers get a playful story about a writer whose invented West refuses to stay on the page.
31833-the-wedge:
H. B. Fyfe's short story The Wedge was printed in If in September 1960. It opens with a man named Barnsley sitting on the floor of a cylindrical chamber, slumped against curving, pearly plastic. He is careful not to glance toward translucent ovals he knows to be observation panels. He is large but thin and bony-faced, in a dirty gray coverall too big except at the shoulders.

When a concealed gong sounds, Barnsley rises and gazes in turn at each of three doors spaced around the chamber, adopting an expression of simple-minded anticipation. Readers get a science-fiction puzzle story whose title gives its clue: finding his way out of this maze is only half the job.
32431-the-model-of-a-judge:
William Morrison's tale, printed in Galaxy in October 1953, centres on Ronar, a reformed former outlaw whom his neighbours still fear and distrust. People move awkwardly near him, and fear looks out of their eyes, though Ronar hopes time will let them see him as one of themselves. At a gathering run by Mrs. Claymore of the Presiding Committee, Mrs. Silver modestly enters a contest, praising the fine women taking part.

The story's joke, set out in its sidenote, asks whether a reformed outlaw could serve as judge when the only verdict concerns a layer cake. Morrison uses a small-town contest and its polite talk to test how far reform, trust, and second chances can go. The tale mixes gentle satire with a serious question about judging others.
32438-the-book-of-courage:
John T. Faris's Book of Courage, published in Philadelphia and London in 1920, opens the Sunrise Inspirational Books series with short readings on courage in everyday life. Its foreword tells of a teacher who fitted a room for children with pictures, plants, goldfish, and a canary. She then faced a cold snap the night before the welcome, when a janitor let the room chill. That small disaster frames the book's question: what courage looks like when plans fail.

Contents divide courage into self-conquest, facing obstacles, industry, facing consequences, courage for others, golden-rule courage, and courage through companionship. Topics include restraining self, forgiving injuries, persisting, toiling, conquering infirmity, truth telling, and duty doing. Faris writes plain, encouraging prose for readers seeking moral examples rather than abstract theory.
32442-gertrude-s-marriage:
W. Heimburg's novel, translated from German by Mrs. J. W. Davis and published in New York in 1889, opens with an unexpected inheritance. Judge Weishaupt teases his friend Assessor Linden, who has just gained a small estate. It holds several hundred acres of meadow and woodland, a wild garden, and a neglected house. Its stock runs to four spavined Andalusian horses, six dried-up old cows, and an old aunt. Linden sits in mute despair before an empty Rhine wine bottle.

From that comic opening, the story follows Linden, Gertrude, and their circle through money, family claims, and the making of a marriage. Heimburg writes with humour about German middle-class life, pride, and affection, as an unwanted estate becomes the ground for a new household. Readers who enjoy domestic novels of manners will find the book warm and readable.
32445-the-pain-and-sorrow-of-evil-marria:
The Pain and Sorrow of Evil Marriage preserves an early humorous tract in verse on marriage. It was reprinted in London in 1840 for the Percy Society from a unique copy printed by Wynkyn de Worde. Its introduction notes three early tracts on the subject, all printed by de Worde, with only one dated, 1535, and the other two assigned to about the same period. Their titles concern those married too soon, those married too late, and the pain and sorrow of evil marriage.

This volume prints the third tract entire, while a brief account of the other two appears in Dibdin's edition of Ames. The Percy Society editors promise a fuller description of these ancient, facetious relics, which mock bad matches with Tudor bluntness. Readers interested in early English verse, printing history, and marriage satire will find a rare, short text in a scholarly reprint.
32501-the-golden-age:
Kenneth Grahame's Golden Age, companion volume to Dream Days and illustrated by Maxfield Parrish, recalls childhood as a world apart from grown-ups, whom children call the Olympians. Published in London and New York in 1900, with copyrights in 1899 and 1904, it opens with a prologue on the Olympians. Chapters follow on holidays, a white-washed uncle, alarms and excursions, and the finding of a princess. Sawdust and sin, young Adam Cupid, burglars, and a harvesting follow.

Later chapters cover snowbound days, what children talked about, Argonauts, and a Roman road. A secret drawer, Exit Tyrannus, a blue room, a falling out, and a Latin farewell follow. Grahame writes from inside a child's imagination, where orchards seem elf-haunted and gardens lead to roofs and adventure. The book remains a classic of childhood memory, warm, witty, and gently rebellious.
32577-dorothy-page:
Eldridge B. Hatcher's Dorothy Page, published in Louisville in 1912, follows a young woman home from college in the North. Dorothy arrives at six-twenty in the evening, beautiful in her neighbor Sterling's eyes, and that night he feels an epoch in his life has occurred.

Sterling, twenty-nine, a Presbyterian elder with a two million dollar fortune, states his case through chapters on conversion, deep water, wronging the little ones, and Baptist principles on the march. Hatcher writes a story of faith, courtship, and conviction, where Dorothy's arrival tests what both families believe.
32701-kant-s-theory-of-knowledge:
H. A. Prichard, Fellow of Trinity College, Oxford, examines Kant's Critique of Pure Reason. His book appeared from the Clarendon Press in 1909. Thirteen chapters move from the problem of the Critique to phenomena and things in themselves. Later chapters treat time and inner sense, knowledge and reality, and the deductions of the categories.

Prichard states Kant's questions plainly. Reason cannot decline questions about God, freedom, and immortality, yet it cannot answer them. He tests each stage of Kant's argument in turn. He presses hardest where Kant assumes what he must prove. The book closes with the postulates of empirical thought and a note refuting idealism.
32764-manners-of-the-age:
H. B. Fyfe tells of Robert, a man living in gracious solitude on a practically deserted Earth, in this story from Galaxy Science Fiction of March 1952, illustrated by Marchetti. Robots serve him: a red tennis robot returns his shots, a referee box calls the game, and serving robots fetch his racket and clothes.

Robert swims in a hundred-foot-square pool and wonders how far he must go to meet another human face to face. It has been ten years since he saw one. A televised invitation brings him to Marcia-Joan, whose robots serve a dinner of raw vegetables and a tiny portion of protein-concentrate. Her robots found the diet in the city library, but they looked up song-birds, not humans.
32803-letters-from-a-father-to-his-son-e:
Charles Franklin Thwing, president of Western Reserve University, writes twelve letters to a son entering college, published by Platt and Peck in 1912. Parts were first read to his own students starting a college year.

The letters treat thought, the essential gentleman, and health as an asset. They treat appreciation, scholarship, and the intellectual life. They treat the use of time, culture, college morals, weakness of character, the genesis of success, and religion. Thwing urges his son to become a thinker. He urges him to choose the better over the good, and the best over the better, and to take time in large pieces, not cut into bits.
32856-lectures-on-the-science-of-languag:
Max Müller delivers nine lectures on the science of language at the Royal Institution of Great Britain in April, May, and June 1861. The volume appeared in New York by Charles Scribner in 1862, from the second London edition, revised. He dedicates the volume to the members of the University of Oxford.

Lectures treat language as a physical science, its growth against its history, and its empirical, classificatory, and theoretical stages. Müller weighs genealogical and morphological classification, comparative grammar, and the origin of language. He quotes Bacon: words shoot back upon the understanding of the wisest, and entangle judgment. Iceland's skalds and fifty thousand inhabitants illustrate his history.
32920-a-question-of-marriage:
Mrs George de Horne Vaizey opens in a London consulting room, where a doctor gives a young woman his hardest advice. She carries a family history he calls a curse, and he tells her plainly that marriage is not for her. Anxiety, depression, and loneliness, he warns, are her worst enemies, and a wife's strains might unbalance her mind. The girl answers only, Thank you.

The novel then tests that ban against living people: Jean, Vanna, and Robert, whose grey eyes and brown eyes exchange an unspoken duel in a railway carriage. Jean, spoiled by Robert's devotion, calls herself a continual enigma to him, puzzling and shocking him by turns. Vanna sticks obstinately to her post between them. The question of the title is whether the doctor's verdict, or the heart, will govern.
32931-harley-greenoak-s-charge:
Bertram Mitford's novel opens on a ship's deck, where Sir Anson Selmes, an elderly, refined baronet, asks a sun-tanned, iron-grey-bearded frontiersman to look after someone in his charge. The second man, hardened by forty-five years in southern Africa, man and boy, accepts with absolute assurance. His keen blue eyes and rough, mahogany-brown hands mark him as a man who has lived by rifle and open country.

The charge of the title becomes Harley Greenoak's trust, and the novel follows what that promise costs him in a land of farms, feuds, and sudden violence. Mitford, at home in colonial Africa, builds his story from that trust and its dangers. It is a period adventure about duty kept under pressure, told with the confidence of a writer who knew the veldt and the men who rode it.
33043-windyridge:
W. Riley's Windyridge, published by Herbert Jenkins in London in 1915, is a Yorkshire novel of moors, farms, and village life. Its chapters open with the call of the heather. A farmer stats his terms, Grace meeting the squire, and a studio, then follow Farmer Brown photographed, a walk over the moor to Romanton. A cynic discourses on woman, and Christmas Day at Windyridge. Widow Robertshaw, Ginty running away, and Barjona falling into a trap carry the plot forward.

Later chapters bring Rose, a carrier's notice to quit, a visit to Zermatt, and a great storm followed by calm after storm, as the heather pulls its people back. Riley writes with affection for moorland folk and their talk, and the novel's humor and sentiment made it popular in its day. It remains a warm, old-fashioned story of a community finding its way through change.
33105-hymns-in-the-chinook-jargon-langua:
Rev. M. Eells, a missionary of the American Missionary Association, compiled Hymns in the Chinook Jargon Language, in a second edition revised and enlarged at Portland, Oregon, in 1889. The hymns grew out of Christian work among Native peoples, and they repeat often because they were meant chiefly for singers who could not read and had to memorize them. Once learners could read, Eells notes, they sang in English.

The book's notes explain its singing practice, as when two syllables must be sung to one note. The examples are nika to the first note of Happy Land, or skookum to one note in another hymn. As a document, it preserves a trade language turned to worship, and the missionary effort to carry hymns across languages. For students of the Pacific Northwest, Native languages, and mission history, it is a small but revealing source.
33409-the-ranch-girls-at-rainbow-lodge:
Margaret Vandercook's Ranch Girls at Rainbow Lodge opens her Ranch Girls series, a set of tales for girls who love horses, ranches, and friendship. The series went on to a pot of gold, boarding school, Europe, home again, and a great adventure, but Rainbow Lodge is where the ranch girls first gather. Vandercook writes with warmth for young readers, in a style that made the series a favorite.

The book's charm lies in its outdoor life, its lively girls, and its sense of a ranch as both home and adventure ground. Its chapters move briskly through rides, scrapes, and good times. For fans of girls' series books, Rainbow Lodge offers a bright, wholesome start to a long and much-loved run.
33554-nancy-of-paradise-cottage:
Shirley Watkins tells the story of Nancy Prescott, a capable girl who keeps house for her sister Alma and manages the shopping, cooking, and daily chores of their cottage home. Alma drifts and daydreams while Nancy plans, and their different tempers shape much of the household comedy. A stern man known to the girls as an ogre, a fashionable visitor, and a school term add new pressures.

Across fifteen chapters Nancy faces quarrels, scrapes, and a great adventure before the cottage itself becomes the center of the story. The novel follows her growth from a hardworking sister into a young woman who can stand up to difficult people and protect the home she loves.
34001-challenge:
Louis Untermeyer published this book of poems in New York in April 1914 with the Century Company. Three sections hold the poems: Summons, Interludes, and Songs of Protest. Early poems include a prayer to arms, a poem on the birth of a child, God's youth in the Berkshire hills, downhill on a bicycle, and midnight by the open window.

Interludes add Sunday night at Kennebunkport, a folk-song in the streets, Isadora Duncan dancing, and a Heretic sequence of blasphemy, irony, mockery, and humility. Songs of Protest close with Caliban in the coal-mines, strikers in the subway, and a voice from the sweat-shops. The book shows a young poet of fire and conscience.
34017-deep-moat-grange:
S. R. Crockett wrote this mystery romance, published in London in 1908 by Hodder and Stoughton. Deep Moat Grange opens with an empty mail gig, a poacher named Davie, a bailiff, and a golden farmer. Elsie, her visitor, a brom-water mystery, an iron trapdoor, and a bricked passage deepen the plot.

Later chapters bring a monks' oven, a breaking dam, comrades in captivity, and a night when Elsie dances for her life. Crockett writes with old-fashioned color and suspense. The novel offers a rich, tangled tale of a moated house and its secrets.
34088-a-poached-peerage:
Sir William Magnay's 1909 novel runs through forty-two chapters of English country life, where a disputed peerage sits at the heart of the plot. Lalage, a young woman met at a village inn, presses a prior claim on a man named Gage. Rival hopes for rank and marriage pull the households around them into open conflict.

The story moves between inn parlours, country houses, and sharp talk among suitors, kin, and hangers-on, as each side works to secure the title. Magnay keeps the tone light and brisk, with comic servants and scheming guests. The question of who truly holds the peerage drives the tale to its close. Readers who enjoy a tale of rank, rivalry, and village wit will find the pace quick and the cast large.
3482-voyages-in-search-of-the-north-west:
This volume draws on Richard Hakluyt's great collection of voyages to tell the search for a northern sea route to Asia. The introduction recalls the editor's own small boat voyage to Arctic seas and his reading of early accounts in Dickens's Household Words. The narratives that follow come from English sailors who sailed toward ice, fog, and unknown coasts.

Readers meet whaling grounds where a hundred Dutch ships might crowd a bay, rival claims to fishing islands, and crews who wintered in harsh places. The book gives the raw material of exploration: logs, letters, and reports rather than a modern history. It suits readers who enjoy first hand adventure and the slow, dangerous opening of the Arctic.
351-of-human-bondage:
W. Somerset Maugham follows Philip Carey from a lonely childhood to adult life in this long novel. Philip, born with a club foot, loses his mother early and grows up under strict kin. He tries school, clerk work, art in Paris, and medicine in London, each path testing his pride and his need for love.

A cruel affair with a waitress named Mildred breaks his heart and his funds more than once, while steadier friends offer a saner path. Maugham writes in plain, steady prose, with little show. The book endures as a study of how a sensitive man learns to live with limits, and to want less yet feel more free.
375-an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce sets this short Civil War tale on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama. A Southern planter, Peyton Farquhar, stands bound with a rope round his neck, guarded by Federal soldiers. As the trap drops, his mind races through a vivid dream of escape, flight through woods, and a rush home to his wife.

Bierce times the dream with care, letting each sense sharpen as Farquhar runs. The final twist snaps the dream shut and restores the grim fact of the bridge. The story endures for its tight craft and its stark view of war, hope, and self-deceit in a few short pages.
439-the-vital-message:
Arthur Conan Doyle argues for spirit contact in this 1919 sequel to The New Revelation, written after the Great War. Doyle claims the war's vast loss opened minds to a new relation with the unseen. He sets out the evidence and the changes he expects in science, faith, and daily life.

Chapters treat the dawning light, the great argument, and the coming world, with notes on spirit photos and clairvoyance. Doyle writes with earnest conviction, as a public man pleading a cause. The book stands as a clear record of his later faith, and of a generation seeking comfort beyond the grave.
4531-the-secret-passage:
Fergus Hume built this detective novel around a cottage, a crime, and a mysterious death, with a secret entrance waiting to explain them. Susan Grant, a parlour-maid of twenty-five, comes to work for the sharp Miss Loach, and the household soon fills with suspects: Lord Caranby, Juliet, Basil, Cuthbert, Mrs. Octagon, and a detective who asks hard questions. Chapters follow the crime, the details, the course of true love, and one mystery after another.

Juliet's story, told in two parts, and Susan's discovery slowly open the hidden passage and the revenge behind it. Hume keeps the plot moving through parlour talk, admissions, and experiments, until nemesis catches the scamp at the centre. Readers get a brisk Edwardian mystery, with romance and detection side by side, and a secret that rewards patience right up to the final chapters.
4613-at-large:
Arthur Christopher Benson published At Large in 1908, as a book of essays by a bachelor tied to college for half the year and free for the other half. He asks what such a man should do with his free months. He cannot live on in college rooms for economy, and he will not drift from house to house like a wandering dove. The essays that follow are his answer, written from a love of independence and quiet study.

Contents run from the scene, contentment, friendship, humour, and travel. They go on to specialism, our lack of great men, shyness, and equality. Later essays cover the dramatic sense, Kelmscott and William Morris, a speech day, literary finish, symbols, optimism, joy, and the love of God. Readers get a calm, civilised set of reflections on how to live well, in Benson's easy, bookish voice.
4723-a-treatise-concerning-the-principle:
George Berkeley, 1685 to 1753, wrote A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge. It inquires into the chief causes of error and difficulty in the sciences, with the grounds of scepticism, atheism, and irreligion. He dedicates the work to Thomas, Earl of Pembroke, knight of the Garter and lord of the privy council. He wonders that an obscure person unknown to his lordship should presume to address him in that manner.

Berkeley argues that a man who writes to promote useful knowledge and religion may properly choose such a patron, since Pembroke ornaments and supports church and learning. His treatise then sets out the idealist philosophy for which he is famous. Material things exist as perceived, and abstract ideas mislead science. Readers get a short, demanding classic of philosophy, best read slowly, with its dedication as a window into its age.
4787-the-story-of-julia-page:
Kathleen Norris published The Story of Julia Page in 1915, with a frontispiece by C. Allan Gilbert. Its pictured line says it never occurred to anyone to ask why the heroine differs from other women, or what made her so. Chapter one opens with Emeline, wife of George Page, slowly reaching, in her thirtieth year, a sullen conviction that life is monstrously unfair.

From resentment at an unhappy marriage, Emeline's mind returns to a pert, precocious childhood and a restless, discontented girlhood, feeling with smouldering fury that she never had a fair chance at all. It took years to reach that conclusion, since Emeline, shrewd among women she knew, was in essential things unintelligent, and mental effort was strange to her. She scrambled through grammar school and five further years of schooling. Readers get a Norris novel of a woman's discontent, marriage, and slow awakening.
481-in-the-bishop-s-carriage:
Miriam Michelson tells of Nancy, a young pickpocket who poses as a Bryn Mawr girl to dodge police, in this brisk novel. After a theft at a station, Nancy slips into a bishop's carriage and talks her way into a new life among polite folk. Her thief friend Tom watches from the shadows, torn between love and the law.

Michelson writes in Nancy's quick, slangy voice, full of nerve and humor. Each chapter tests whether Nancy can keep her act, or fall back to the streets. The novel charms as a tale of disguise and second chances, where a sharp girl outwits both cops and society.
5129-the-prodigal-judge:
Vaughan Kester's novel is set in the pine woods of the American South after the Civil War, where the last of the Quintard family has died at the old Barony house. A boy left at the margins of that household crosses paths with a wandering judge, river men, and tavern fighters, and the story follows their fortunes toward Tennessee.

Courtroom scenes, raft journeys, shooting matches, and jailbreaks give the book the flavour of a Southern picaresque. Beneath the adventure, Kester tells a story of inheritance, loyalty. Second chances follow, as a rootless judge and a homeless boy each look for a place to belong.
5131-childe-harold-s-pilgrimage:
Lord Byron's long poem follows Childe Harold, a weary young nobleman, on a pilgrimage through Europe in four cantos. Harold travels from Portugal and Spain to Greece, the Alps, Italy, and Rome, and Byron uses each place to reflect on history, liberty, war, and the ruins of empires.

The poem made Byron famous overnight, and its melancholy traveller became a model for Romantic heroes. Readers will find famous passages on Waterloo, Venice, and Rome, alongside Byron's own voice breaking through Harold's, as the poet turns a journey into a meditation on his age.
5183-the-unexpurgated-case-against-woman:
Sir Almroth E. Wright's 1913 treatise argues against giving women the parliamentary vote in Britain. Its three parts first answer the arguments for suffrage, from natural rights, justice, and taxation. They then present Wright's own case, resting on what he calls woman's disability in physical force, intellect, and public morality. Finally they consider the wider aims of the suffrage movement.

Wright, a distinguished physician, wrote at the height of the suffragette campaign. His book is now read as a document of opposition rather than as a persuasive case. It offers a clear, if dated, view of the arguments suffragists had to defeat before the vote was won.
534-an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France in this early travel book. With his friend Cigarette, Stevenson paddles the Sambre and Oise canals, past Antwerp, Maubeuge, and Noyon, camping, portaging, and dining with canal folk. A preface jokes that a small book needs a large welcome.

Stevenson writes with light, witty prose, keen on rain, inns, and cathedral towns. The voyage is less about distance than about talk and temper on the water. The book charms as a young writer's ramble, where a canoe proves a fine lens for foreign life.
5430-preface-to-a-dictionary-of-the-engl:
Samuel Johnson wrote this preface for his great Dictionary of the English Language, published in the mid-eighteenth century. He begins with the lonely labor of the dictionary-maker, a worker driven more by fear of failure than hope of praise, and considered a servant of learning rather than its master. The preface explains what he set out to do and why the task was so hard.

Johnson defends his choices about spelling, meaning, and usage, admitting where the language resisted order. Readers get both a window into eighteenth-century English and a famous piece of literary prose. It remains the best short introduction to how one man tried to fix a living language in print.
5706-time-and-change:
John Burroughs reflects on nature, science, and faith in Time and Change, published in Boston and New York in 1912. His preface warns readers plainly that the volume holds more hard science and scientific speculation than spiritual comfort, as if offering a stone where bread was asked. Essays that follow weigh what changing knowledge does to old beliefs about the natural world.

Burroughs writes as a field observer turned thinker, grounding large questions in birds, seasons, and country walks. Readers who enjoy nature writing with a philosophical edge will find calm, clear prose and honest doubt. The book appeals to those who want to see how a naturalist of his generation faced new science without giving up wonder at the living world.
6030-the-iron-star-and-what-it-saw-on-it:
John Preston True invites girls and boys and their elders to follow an Iron Star across the ages, from myth to history. His preface calls the world a wonderful place, grown day by day and century by century a little better worth living in, like a fairy story with the advantage of being true.

None of us saw the world's beginning, True admits, but scholars have worked the problem backward through the years. Starting from a good dry spot and following the star's wanderings, readers stay near the truth of how people lived long ago. The book teaches history as a journey, not a list.
6055-the-bobbsey-twins-at-snow-lodge:
Laura Lee Hope sends the Bobbsey twins to Snow Lodge for winter holidays, opening with runaways and a question from little Flossie: will Snap pull them, and give a good ride? Freddie, fastening the big shaggy dog to his sled with a homemade harness, answers with wisdom that Snap pulled fine on trial.

Chapters follow old Mr. Carford, a big snowball, an accusation, the story of Snow Lodge, unwelcome news, a snow slide, and lost children in the woods. Snap goes missing, a big storm hits, a tree falls, and missing money appears. The twins' winter adventure mixes snow play with a small mystery.
6695-tales-of-the-jazz-age:
F. Scott Fitzgerald gathers his Jazz Age tales in a 1922 Scribner volume, with a table that groups them as My Last Flappers and other sets. The Jelly-Bean, a Southern story set in Tarleton, Georgia, drew scolding letters from all over the South, Fitzgerald notes with affection for his town. Each tale first ran in magazines like Vanity Fair, Metropolitan, and Smart Set.

Flappers, jelly-beans, and bright young folk move through parties, love affairs, and sudden falls. Fitzgerald writes with a lyric ease that made his name. Tales of the Jazz Age is a sparkling, bittersweet set, capturing the 1920s at their gayest and most hollow.
6858-grace-harlowe-s-second-year-at-over:
Jessie Graham Flower brings Grace Harlowe back for a second year at Overton College in 1914. Overton claims her own, the unforeseen strikes, Mrs. Elwood comes to the rescue, and a belated freshman arrives. An anarchist chooses a roommate, Elfreda makes a rash promise, and girls and their ideals fill the early chapters.

An offended freshman, a finger of suspicion, a summons, and Grace holding court lead to mercy, reform, and Christmas children. Grace makes a resolution and confesses a fault before the close. Grace Harlowe's Second Year is a warm, old-style college tale of friendship, honor, and growth.
6897-the-little-savage:
Captain Marryat left this adventure tale unfinished at his death, and the introduction explains how it reached print. Marryat wrote the first part and two chapters of the second, carrying the story to chapter twenty four. His son Frank Marryat then edited the volume and supplied a short preface to the second part.

The book stands as the last work of a popular sea writer, sent to press while its author lay in long illness. Readers meet a tale cut short by death and finished by a son's care, rather than a smooth whole. That broken history gives the volume its special interest for lovers of Marryat's sea stories.
6899-the-children-s-pilgrimage:
Two children sit on a doorstep on an autumn Sunday evening in a quiet old court behind Bloomsbury, with a mongrel dog gazing at them with hungry, loving eyes. The elder, a girl of ten, and her brother of eight look clean and respectable, not like waifs of the East End. Their street is a cul de sac leading nowhere, and at that hour it seems quite deserted.

Mrs Meade calls the first part Looking for the Guide, and the hymn line at its head sets the tone of a search. The children are alone in the world in a way the opening makes plain, and the tale follows their pilgrimage step by step. It is a story of trust, care, and a long road walked by small feet.
6916-english-men-of-letters-coleridge:
H D Traill writes the life of Coleridge for the English Men of Letters series, facing a subject of many sides. His preface quotes De Quincey on Coleridge's multiform attainments and powers, and on the many demands they make on any biographer. De Quincey's praise is touched with humor, Traill admits, but in substance it is just, and it excuses the shortcomings of a short volume.

No complete life of Coleridge on any large scale then existed, and no full critical account of his work stood ready to hand. Traill therefore works within narrow limits, sketching the poet, thinker, and talker in brief compass. The book serves as a compact guide to a man whose genius spilled across poetry, thought, and talk.
7353-birds-in-town-village:
W. H. Hudson's Birds in Town and Village reworks his first book about bird life, Birds in a Village from 1893, with affection and a critic's hand. Hudson explains in his preface that the reissue let him mend faults in the portions he kept and throw out a good deal of matter not worth keeping. The first portion, Birds in a Village, was mostly rewritten with fresh matter added.

The book joins town and village birds with impressions of rural scenes in England, written by an author who cherished his first book above others. Hudson watches sparrows, songbirds, and village life with a naturalist's patience and a poet's ear. Readers get a revised classic of English bird writing, kept and improved by its author.
7401-a-crystal-age:
W. H. Hudson's romance of the future begins with a feeling most readers know: dissatisfaction with the present order, joined to a vague hope that something better may come. His preface warns that any picture of the future must be false, since we cannot imagine what we have never known. Yet the attempt itself, he argues, has a perennial interest.

The story that follows imagines a future people living in pastoral simplicity, far from the noise and machinery of Hudson's own age. A traveler finds their world and learns its customs, its loves, and its limits. The novel is less a blueprint than a dream: a quiet, beautiful society held up as a mirror to the restless nineteenth century that produced it.
7433-the-awkward-age:
Henry James's novel of 1899 is an experiment in pure talk. Almost the whole book is dialogue, with hardly any narration to explain what the speakers mean. The awkward age of the title is the age of Nanda Brookenham. She is a young woman in London society, no longer a child and not yet safely married. She stands caught between her mother's fashionable circle and her own conscience.

Around Nanda gather her mother, Mrs. Brookenham, the faithful Mr. Longdon, and the charming Vanderbank, all talking brilliantly and revealing themselves by what they say and withhold. James's preface calls the book's germ small beside the mass it grew into, and the growth is all in conversation. It is a demanding, dazzling novel of manners, best read slowly, listening hard.
7832-the-deluge:
David Graham Phillips's The Deluge opens with Mr. Blacklock, then moves through kings arising, a woman's arrival, a candidate for respectability, danger signals, and gentlemen in quotes. Blacklock goes into training, trails Langdon, and meets pillars of society who prove hollow.

Later chapters bring Anita, a genteel hold-up, a windfall from Gentleman Joe, a conspiracy against Anita, and Black Matt's triumph. The novel opens with a jest on Napoleon and a faked royal genealogy, then turns to American finance, politics, and love, where money floods like a deluge over old morals.
7972-homer-and-his-age:
Andrew Lang wrote this study as a follow-up to his earlier Homer and the Epic, taking up the critics who doubted that one poet made the Iliad and Odyssey. He examines the alleged discrepancies in the poems, the case for Homeric unity, and what the epics reveal about the age that produced them. An editor's note warns that unclear typesetting in the original left some passages marked with gaps.

Lang argues from the poems themselves, testing whether one mind could hold their world together. His prose is clear and combative, aimed at general readers as well as scholars. The book still serves as a spirited defence of Homer as a poet rather than a committee, and as an introduction to the long debate over who wrote the epics.
8208-poems-of-coleridge:
Arthur Symons selected and arranged these poems of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, with an introduction and notes. His contents span the poet's career: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, Christabel, Kubla Khan, Lewti, The Ballad of the Dark Ladie, Love, Dejection: An Ode, France: An Ode. Fears in Solitude, This Lime-Tree Bower My Prison, Frost at Midnight, The Nightingale, The Eolian Harp, Hymn Before Sun-Rise, Youth and Age, and Work Without Hope, among many others.

Symons's selection gives the essential Coleridge in one volume, from supernatural ballads to meditative conversation poems. His introduction places the poet among the Romantics and explains his uneven, brilliant career. For readers new to Coleridge, this is the ideal starting point, and for old readers, a well-chosen companion.
8489-specimens-of-the-table-talk-of-samu:
This volume gathers specimens of the table talk of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, dedicated to James Gillman of the Grove, Highgate, and to Mrs. Gillman, who housed the poet in his later years. Coleridge's talk, recorded by listeners, ranges over poetry, philosophy, religion, and politics, in the brilliant, digressive style that made his conversation famous.

A note warns that Greek transliterations in the file are missing or suspect, but the English talk survives in full. Readers meet Coleridge the talker, not only the poet of the Ancient Mariner, thinking aloud at table. The book is a primary source for Romantic conversation, and for Coleridge's mind in its freest form.
8668-revenge:
Robert Barr packs twenty-one tales of payback into this collection, from An Alpine Divorce and Which Was the Murderer? to A Dynamite Explosion, An Electrical Slip, and The Vengeance of the Dead. Illustrations promise a safe blown open, a cord dangling above a policeman's head, and a bomb launched outward, and the stories deliver on that melodramatic billing. Over the Stelvio Pass, a deal on change, a modern Samson, and the exposure of Lord Stansford keep the settings shifting.

Barr writes with a journalist's briskness and a showman's sense of the twist, letting revenge arrive by law, by accident, by science, or by sheer nerve. The tales are short, sharp, and built for a single sitting each. Fans of Victorian sensation fiction will enjoy the variety, and the collection shows how the revenge plot, old as drama itself, adapted to dynamite, electricity, and the modern city.
9194-the-second-deluge:
Garrett Serviss wrote this science romance in 1912 about a second deluge drowning the world. Cosmo Versál mocks fate, then watches the first drops fall and the world swept with terror. A third sign leads to selecting the flower of mankind, and waters rise as crowds storm the ark. New York faces its last day, and a billion is bid for a share.

The ark sails over drowned Europe, to Paris under the sea and adventures in Colorado, as a terrible nucleus nears. Serviss mixes astronomy with adventure. The novel remains a lively early disaster tale, vast in scale and Victorian in wonder.
94-alexander-s-bridge:
Bartley Alexander builds great bridges and a great reputation, then risks both for an old love. Willa Cather's Alexander's Bridge, her first novel, follows the engineer between Boston, London, and the Canadian west. Professor Wilson watches his friend's rise with quiet doubt.

Alexander's marriage to Winifred steadies him, while Hilda Burgoyne, an actress from his youth, unsettles him. The bridge he designs becomes a test of nerve and character. An epilogue closes the story after disaster. The short novel shows Cather finding her voice. Cather later called it a study in divided loyalty, and critics still debate its hero.
9415-olaf-the-glorious-a-story-of-the-vi:
Robert Leighton wrote this Viking age story around Olaf the Glorious, opening with the finding of Olaf. In early summer, Sigurd Erikson journeys north into Esthonia to gather the king's taxes. In a seaport on the Gulf of Finland, tall, strong, and fair-haired, with armed servants in train, he rides across the marketplace toward the sea.

Fishing boats put out with the tide, merchant vessels lie at anchor, and a long dragonship waits near the strand. Leighton fills the tale with voyages, battles, and Norse honor. The book remains a rousing boys' adventure of the Viking world, vivid and swift.
a-crystal-age:
W. H. Hudson framed A Crystal Age as a romance of the future. his preface admits every such dream is built from the dreamer's own age — in his case, the cults and crazes of the 1880s. His narrator, out botanizing, falls into a ravine, is buried by falling earth, and wakes after a long unconsciousness in a changed world.

The future he finds is a quiet, communal household in a great house amid rich country, where people live close to nature and find his modern habits strange. Love in that ordered world follows rules he cannot accept, and his feeling for a daughter of the house drives the story to its close. Hudson's utopia is pastoral rather than mechanical, a dream of life returned to the soil.
a-straight-deal-or-the-ancient-grudge:
Owen Wister, the novelist of the American West, turns to public argument in nineteen chapters about England and America after the First World War. He begins with the flood of angry letters that any printed opinion now brings. His own opinion is plain: the old grudge between the two peoples should end.

Chapter by chapter he takes up wartime complaints, old history taught badly in schools, Irish questions, and slights remembered on both sides of the Atlantic. He grants faults to each country and asks readers to weigh the record fairly. The book is a plea for friendship between the English-speaking peoples, written in a plain, combative style.
a-treatise-concerning-the-principles-of-:
George Berkeley's Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge inquires into the causes of error in the sciences. Its title page adds the grounds of scepticism, atheism, and irreligion to the charge sheet. Berkeley dedicates the work to the Earl of Pembroke. His preface asks the reader to suspend judgment until the whole is read through once.

Berkeley argues that things exist only as they are perceived by a mind. Matter, as philosophers imagined it, is an empty abstraction behind our ideas. From this he builds proofs of God's existence and the soul's immateriality. An introduction attacks abstract ideas before the principles begin. The treatise made its young Irish author a founder of idealism, the doctrine that reality is mental. Few philosophy books so short have argued so long.
alexander-s-bridge:
Willa Cather's first novel centers on Bartley Alexander, a celebrated bridge builder at the height of his fame. The story opens with Professor Lucius Wilson, who taught Alexander, arriving in Boston and looking up his former student. Wilson's visit frames the portrait of a man whose public triumph rests on a strained marriage and an old love not fully buried.

In ten chapters and an epilogue, Alexander moves between Boston, London, and the great bridge he is building in Canada. A chance reunion with Hilda Burgoyne, the actress he loved before his marriage, reopens what his success had closed. Cather keeps the scale small and the prose exact. This printing also includes Alfred Noyes's poem The Barrel Organ after the novel.
ammianus-marcellinus-roman-history-yonge:
Ammianus Marcellinus, a retired Roman officer, wrote his history of the empire in the late fourth century. C. D. Yonge translated the surviving books into English. Much of the full work is lost, but the remainder is rich.

The surviving books run from Constantius through the reign of Valens. Emperor Julian's Persian campaign receives a long, admiring account from a near witness. Ammianus writes with a soldier's eye for terrain, weather, and morale. Historians rank him as the last great historian of Rome. His pages remain a prime source for the late empire.
among-the-trees-at-elmridge: Ella Rodman Church takes young readers among the trees at Elmridge, opening with a spring opening and moving to maples, elms, and old acquaintances. Each chapter introduces a tree by its leaves, bark, and habits, in talk suited to children. The book makes botany a friendly outdoor lesson, learned tree by tree.
amours-de-voyage:
Arthur Hugh Clough wrote his verse tale as a set of letters in English hexameters, and this text follows the 1903 Macmillan edition. The speaker, Claude, travels in Italy while Rome is in turmoil, and writes to his friend Eustace about sights, doubts, and a young woman he keeps meeting. He is clever, restless, and unable to commit to anything.

Across five cantos the letters move from Rome to Florence and the hills, mixing travel notes with shy courtship. Claude questions faith, duty, love, and his own hesitation, often with dry humor. The poem is prized for sounding like real modern thought, unsure and self-mocking, inside old verse forms.
an-inland-voyage:
Robert Louis Stevenson's first book recounts a canoe trip through Belgium and France. His friend Walter Simpson went with him. The dedication addresses Simpson as the Cigarette. The contents chart the route. It runs from Antwerp to Boom, then down the Willebroek Canal. It passes the Royal Sport Nautique and the canalized Sambre, past Maubeuge and Landrecies. At last it follows the Oise in flood, through Compiègne to Précy.

Two young men in canoes are taken for pedlars. Rain soaks them again and again. Innkeepers and canal folk feed and amuse them. Stevenson turns discomfort into comedy. He watches bargemen, lock-keepers, and the flat green country with care. Travel for its own sake is the subject. The book sets out the wandering voice that runs through all his later work.
an-occurrence-at-owl-creek-bridge:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this short story of the Civil War, told in three numbered parts. It opens on a railroad bridge in northern Alabama, where a man stands with a rope around his neck, hands bound, watched by Federal soldiers and a captain. The drop is about to be taken from under his feet. Bierce stays close to the physical facts: the boards, the sentinels, the cannon on the slope.

The condemned man is Peyton Farquhar, a planter who tried to burn the bridge for the Confederacy. As the plank tips, the story follows his sharpening senses and what seems to be an escape through the creek and the woods home. Bierce's ending reframes everything before it, and the tale has become the classic example of the tricked point of view in short fiction.
at-large:
E. W. Hornung published this novel with Scribner's in 1902, between his famous Raffles stories of the amateur cracksman. Hornung here leaves burglary aside for a drama of suspicion inside respectable English life. A colonel, a forceful lady visitor, and a man named Dick drive the early tension, as an identification at a doorway stops a door mid-swing.

Dialogue carries the book: interviews, challenges, and guarded answers slowly expose what each person knows. The colonel's cry of recognition, and the lady's anger on the other side of the door, show Hornung's method of letting manners crack under pressure. Readers who know Raffles will find the same crisp scenes and reversals, turned toward reputation and doubt rather than crime for sport.
at-whispering-pine-lodge:
Lawrence J. Leslie published this boys' adventure in 1919, sending four chums into the Adirondacks for a stay at a fur farmer's lodge. Max leads the party; Touch-and-Go Steve slips off with his steel-jointed fishing rod whenever work calls. Bandy-legs and the others complete the team of outdoor boys.

Their host Obed Grimes keeps a lodge of many wonders, stocked with the products of his fur farm. Night prowlers threaten the stock, so traps, taps on the cabin wall, and a tree bearing strange fruit supply the mysteries. Steve's dream comes true before the fur farmer's triumph closes the tale. Leslie writes brisk series fiction: camping craft, animal lore, and small dangers solved by plucky teamwork.
birds-in-town-village:
W. H. Hudson's Birds in Town and Village revises and enlarges his first book about bird life, Birds in a Village, first published in 1893. Hudson rewrote the first portion with fresh observations, threw out matter he judged unworthy, and added an entirely new part on birds in a Cornish village.

Five shorter essays between the two long parts are retained with little alteration, in one or two instances covering the same ground as the new matter. Hudson writes of English rural scenes with the affection of a first book's author, mending faults where he found them. Bird lovers and readers of English nature writing will find this a mellow, observant volume.
by-conduct-and-courage: By Conduct and Courage, G, a, henty's tale, the brave conduct. This book preserves that adventure. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
by-shore-and-sedge:
Bret Harte gathered three California tales in By Shore and Sedge, pieces from the mining frontier he made famous. An Apostle of the Tules opens on a camp meeting in Tasajara Valley in October 1856, four hundred settlers camped in a dreary marsh for a religious revival. Harte watches preachers, sick families, and scoffing boys with his usual mix of irony and pity.

Sarah Walker and A Ship of '49 complete the volume, the last reaching back to the gold rush year itself. Harte's California is a place of sudden gatherings, rough faith, and stranger kindness. These shorter pieces show his method at its purest: a vivid scene, a twist of character, and sentiment kept on a tight rein.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alain-rene-le:
Alain-Rene Le Sage was a writer born at Sarzeau, Morbihan, in 1668, who died at Boulogne-sur-Mer in 1747. Son of a notary who died early, he left the Jesuit college of Vannes penniless, his guardian having squandered his fortune. Marriage came at twenty-six; practised law briefly, then devoted himself to literature.

The Abbe de Lyonne gave him a small pension and encouraged Spanish study. He translated Spanish plays without public favour. His farce Crispin rival de son maitre won marked success in 1707 and stays on the stage. Actors' enmity drove him to the Foire theatre, for which he wrote about a hundred plays. Besides Crispin, Turcaret, Le Diable Boiteux, and Gil Blas deserve special mention. Turcaret ou le Financier, 1709, is a prose comedy about a financier. Gil Blas, despite assertion, is no Spanish plagiarism but an original work counted among France's romance masterpieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alger-of-lieg:
Alger of Liège, learned French priest born at Liège about 1055, died at Cluny in 1132. He studied at Liège, became Deacon of St. Bartholomew's, and about 1100 Canon of St. Lambert's cathedral, where he stayed twenty years. In 1121 he retired to Cluny's monastery and died there.

His treatise against Berengarius's heresy, De sacramento corporis et sanguinis Domini, won high esteem from Peter of Cluny and Erasmus. His other writings: De misericordia et justitia, a Fathers anthology with brief commentaries, a free-will treatise, and one on the Mass's sacrifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-all-hallows-c:
All Hallows College prepares priests for the missions in English-speaking countries. In 1840 the young Dublin priest John Hand lived with a Vincentian community, unbound by its rules. He resolved to found a missionary college. The project seemed fanciful for one so young, unknown, and penniless, but Hand trusted Heaven and Irish generosity. He won Gregory XVI's approbation at Rome. With O'Connell's aid he leased a mansion and twenty-six acres north of Dublin, once the Priory of All Hallows' land.

On 1 November 1842, with Archbishop Murray's encouragement, Hand formally opened the college and gave it its present name. For four years he served as president, directing studies, establishing finances, and organizing staff. Then, worn out by labours, above all by collecting funds house to house and parish to parish, he died in the spring of 1846. He left the harvest to others. His ideal was that All Hallows should be apostolic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altar-ledge:
The altar ledge began as a step raised slightly behind the plain table-shaped altar, holding candlesticks, flowers, reliquaries, and other ornaments. Later the tabernacle joined the altar as a stationary appendage, with further steps at its sides and behind it. These steps are also called degrees or gradini, their fronts sometimes beautifully painted and decorated.

Brunelleschi's Santo Spirito in Florence shows gradini with beautiful miniature groups from the Passion of Christ. The ledge thus marks the altar's growth from bare table to a stepped setting for ornaments and tabernacle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-altarage:
Altarage comes from the low Latin altaragium, revenue reserved for the chaplain, or altarist, as against the parish priest's income. The distinction once guarded the chaplain's livelihood apart from the parish priest's own benefice and income. Today it means the fees a priest receives from the laity for functions performed for them, such as marriages, baptisms, funerals, and other rites.

It is also termed honorarium, stipend, stole fee, or altarage itself in modern use. Each name marks the same payment: a free offering for a priest's personal service at life's turning points.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-of-lie:
An eleventh-century Belgian chronicler, Anselm of Liège was born in 1008 and died about 1056. Liège's famous episcopal school educated him, and he became canon and dean of the cathedral, where Bishop Wazo was his friend. His chronicle, the Gesta Episcoporum Tungrensium, Trajectensium, et Leodiensium, ranks among the best of its period for literary merit and historical value.

It carries on Heriger of Lobbes's work, which covered the first twenty-seven bishops, from Saint Maternus to Remaclus. Anselm wrote at the request of his godmother, Countess Ida, Abbess of Saint Cecilia at Cologne, adding the lives of twenty-five more bishops, down to Wazo. Wazo gets a very full and particular account. The latest edition of the Gesta appears in Monumenta Germaniae Historica: Scriptores, VII, 161-234, and also XIV, 107-120, from 1883. Anselm's style is clear, and his zeal for church reform matches his critical intelligence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-josep:
Antoine-Joseph Mege, a Maurist Benedictine born at Clermont in 1625, spent his life in prayer, preaching, and study. He joined the Benedictines at Vendome in 1643, taught theology at Saint-Denis, and served as prior at Rethel. Late in life he withdrew to Saint-Germain-des-Pres near Paris, dividing his days between prayer and books.

His chief work commented on the Rule of Saint Benedict, attacking the strict reading of Abbot Rance of La Trappe. Maurist superiors banned the commentary in 1689 at the urging of Bossuet. He also translated Saint Ambrose on virginity and wrote a work on Christian morals, leaving a small but sharp body of monastic writing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anton-berlage:
Anton Berlage, a German dogmatic theologian born at Munster in 1805, taught at his native city's academy until his death in 1881. Early teachers drew him toward risky speculation, but study at Tubingen under Drey, Hirscher, and Mohler turned him to a historical method. Ordained in 1832 without seminary training, he lectured first on apologetics and morals, then on dogma alone.

His seven-volume Catholic Dogmatics, published between 1839 and 1864, gathered his teaching in clear and elegant form. Pupils praised his concise and direct lectures, and his spirit shaped the whole faculty at Munster. The entry presents a teacher whose steady orthodoxy steadied German theology in a restless age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolic-col:
The Apostolic College means the Twelve Apostles as a body commissioned by Christ to spread the reign of God over the whole world. They are founders, foundation, and supports of the visible church on earth, and the name apostle marks their commission. An apostle is a missionary sent by proper authority to carry the gospel to new lands, a meaning fixed by the sending of the Twelve. To call them a college implies they worked together under one head for one purpose.

Referring readers to the article on Apostles for scriptural treatment, this entry deals with dogmatic aspects, the doctrines behind accredited envoys and teachers. Christ, it argues, founded a teaching, governing, and serving apostolate whose charter lies in the gospel commissions. The piece suits readers who want the theology behind the Twelve, not just their names and stories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-banns-of-marr:
Banns of marriage are the church's public announcement of the names of people planning to marry. The word comes from Latin bannum and Old English bannan, to summon. Their object is to uncover any impediment to the marriage and to tell all interested parties of its near celebration. From Christian society's start, marriage counted as a public religious act under church control.

Notice to the bishop dates to the second century, and later the parish priest took up the duty with reputable parishioners' help. Publishing names in church seems to have begun in France near the end of the twelfth century. It was already Gallican custom in 1215, when Innocent III mentioned it to Beauvais's bishop. That same year the Fourth Lateran Council made banns a general law of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-age:
Canonical age is the year fixed by church law at which a person becomes able to take on duties. He may enjoy privileges, enter states of life, hold office, or receive sacraments. Each such act needs growth of mind and body fitted to free acceptance, with knowledge of its duties. The Church sets the age at which one is generally thought qualified. Less growth suffices for baptism than for marriage or priesthood, and higher offices demand more.

Jurists split life into seven ages. They are infancy to seven, childhood to fourteen, puberty to twenty-five, and majority to forty. Manhood runs to fifty or sixty, old age to seventy, and decrepitude to a hundred or death, each year complete. Old discipline varied by time and place. Gratian set seven for tonsure and the first minor orders, twelve for acolyte, twenty for subdeaconship, and thirty for deaconship, later 25.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carthage:
Carthage was a Phoenician colony that long rivaled Rome for mastery of the civilized world before a Roman army destroyed it in 146 B.C. Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 B.C. as a Roman colony, and it became capital of Africa Nova, a province that grew rich and flourishing. African Christianity opens in 180 with martyrs at Scillium and Madaura, and within twenty years a thriving church stood at Carthage.

Tertullian, born at Carthage about 160, defended the faith in his Apology of about 197, claiming Christians had filled every corner of African life. Cyprian, elected bishop in 249, stands with Tertullian as the great figure of the early church there. Later sections trace the primacy of Carthage, its councils, and its bishops. Leo XIII restored the archdiocese in 1884 under Cardinal Lavigerie, who revived Christian life on the ancient site.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-dufre:
Charles Dufresne du Cange was a historian and philologist born at Amiens in 1610 and dead at Paris in 1688. His father, a magistrate, had him taught by the Jesuits at Amiens. He studied law at Orléans and joined the Bar before the Parlement of Paris in 1631. The law did not satisfy him, so he returned to Amiens, married in 1638, and in 1645 bought his father-in-law's post as Treasurer of France.

Neither office nor a family of ten children kept him from scholarship. Conversant with many languages, he was consulted from all sides and gathered much through correspondence. His energy went largely to the history of France and of Constantinople. Two great works grew from that preparation, above all his glossary of medieval and late Latin writers, published at Paris in three folio volumes in 1678.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-b:
An entry on Christopher Bainbridge, Archbishop of York and cardinal, born near Appleby about 1464. He entered Queen's College, Oxford, became its provost before 1495 and a doctor of laws, and later gave generously to the college. He held many benefices, including the London treasurership and the Mastership of the Rolls. Henry the Seventh named him Bishop of Durham in 1507, and the pope moved him to York in 1508.

Sent by Henry the Eighth as ambassador to Rome in 1509, Bainbridge was made cardinal by Julius the Second in March 1511 for winning Henry to the pope against France. He led a papal expedition that besieged Ferrara with success, and he sought the title Most Christian King for Henry after Louis of France forfeited it. In July 1514 his steward, the priest Rinaldo de Modena, poisoned him in revenge for a blow, and Bainbridge was buried in the English Hospice at Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cities-of-ref:
The cities of refuge were towns where Jewish law gave asylum to anyone who had killed another without intent, sheltering him from the avenger of blood. Under blood-revenge, a victim's kinsman held it a duty to kill the slayer, intentional or not. The six biblical cities were Cedes in Galilee, Sichem in Mount Ephraim, and Hebron in the south, west of Jordan, with Bosor, Ramoth in Galaad, and Gaulon in Basan to the east.

Three western cities seem to have come first, probably under Josias, with the eastern three added when Jews spread wider after the Exile. Protection was conditional: the fugitive had to prove his deed unpremeditated, then stay within the city's bounds, unable to return home or buy off the avenger. An intentional killer found no refuge even at God's altar, and might be dragged from it to death, as Joab was.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civil-marriag:
In municipal law marriage is not a contract in the strict sense but a civil status. It unites one man and one woman legally for life, with rights and duties assigned by the law of matrimony. It is presumed to serve the State's highest interest, so the law encourages it, holds it permanent, and dissolves it only by death or, where statutes allow, by divorce. Consent of the parties is essential to a valid marriage.

In England solemnisation before a clergyman was required until 1836, except for Quakers and Jews, when civil and dissenter marriages were legalised. Common-law ages of consent were fourteen for males and twelve for females, and the act of 1753 voided underage marriages lacking parental consent. The article surveys formalities, annulment for deception or duress, and foreign rules, from Scotland's irregular marriages by mere consent to Germany's higher ages and Quebec's parental consent under twenty-one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-college:
Robert Schwickerath's wide survey starts from the word college itself, from the Latin collegium. At first it meant a community, a corporation, or a body of colleagues in a common pursuit. Rome knew guilds of artisans as collegia, plus groups joined for worship or mutual aid. Official bodies bore the name too, such as the College of Pontiffs. The sense survives in modern bodies like the College of Physicians and the College of Surgeons.

From the fourteenth century the word often meant a community of secular clergy living on a foundation for religious service. Schwickerath treats England, where the collegiate system still marks Oxford and Cambridge, and notes Winchester College, founded in 1379 as the first college outside a university. He follows the humanist influence, the colleges of Paris, and the American college, long the main home of liberal education and now in a state of transition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-concubinage:
H. A. Gaynor's entry defines concubinage today as a more or less permanent state of a man and woman living in illicit intercourse. Strictly it covers unions where neither party is bound by vow, marriage, Holy Orders, or kinship. Dwelling together does not matter. Repetition or continuance of illicit relations between the same persons forms the essence. The term, however, has not always meant the same thing.

In the Old Testament a legitimate spouse of lower rank, or a bondwoman, might be called concubine without denying her marriage. The label marked her lesser share in rank, property, and household rule. Roman law and early church records used a like sense: a quasi-wife, recognized by law under set terms. Toledo's council of 400 legislated for laymen on the matter. With Rome's fall and Roman law's decline, lawful concubinage faded, and the word took its modern illicit sense.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-o:
This reference entry covers two councils held at Orange in southern France, the first in 441 and the second in 529, and explains why the second matters far beyond its region. It sets each meeting in its place, names its president and bishops, and lists the subjects its canons addressed.

The first council, under Hilary of Arles, issued thirty canons on the sacraments, sanctuary, relations among bishops, catechumens, and the marriage of clergy. Far more important was the second council, presided over by Caesarius of Arles, the first in Gaul to issue a decision on a matter of faith. Its rulings on grace and free will shaped Western teaching for centuries, and the entry points readers to the acts and modern studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-deluge:
A long scriptural entry treats the Deluge, the catastrophe fully described in Genesis chapters 6 to 9 and recalled across Scripture from Wisdom to Second Peter. It considers the biblical account, its historicity, the Flood's universality, and collateral questions in turn. Genesis tells how God, seeing human wickedness, spared Noah's family, commanded an ark, and sent forty days' rain, with waters prevailing 150 days.

Critics read the account as a mosaic of two flood stories, Yahwistic and Priestly, differing in authorship and detail. Historicity weighs four theories, from mere fancy to borrowing, against flood legends worldwide. Universality asks whether the Flood covered the whole earth or destroyed all men over part of it. Time, place, and natural causes follow, with dates from rival texts and Babylonian parallels in the Tigris-Euphrates valley.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demiurge:
A philosophy entry defines the demiurge, literally a public worker, a word first used for any craftsman serving the public. Soon other words took the common artisan, while demiurge was reserved for the Great Artificer, the Architect of the universe. At first writers added of the world to distinguish him, but gradually demiurge alone meant the Maker of heaven and earth, as in Plato's Timaeus.

Strictly the word never meant one producing from nothing, for which Greeks used ktistes, but only a maker who shapes and models given matter. Heathen philosophy always presupposes matter, and its world-maker need not be the supreme God. In Gnosticism the Demiurge became a central figure. He stands apart from the Supreme God, and often hostile to him, as the flawed maker of the material world. Other writings, by contrast, identify him with the Highest God himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
An ecclesiastical judge is a churchman holding church jurisdiction, whether in the broad sense or the strict. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that the official body set by lawful authority to administer justice is called a court, tribunal, or audience. Every court holds at least two sworn officers, the judge who decides and the clerk who keeps the record of proceedings and judgment.

As a rule, however, a church court forms a collegiate tribunal, whose members either join the president in deciding as judges or advise him as councillors and assessors. The entry cites Hergenrother-Hollweck, Laurentius, and Sagmuller on the shape of church courts. It gives students of canon law the personnel of justice in short compass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-james-c:
Henry James Coleridge, a writer and preacher born in Devonshire in 1822, was grandson of the poet's brother, son of a King's Bench judge. After Eton and a career at Trinity and Oriel, Oxford, he took Anglican orders in 1848 and joined the Tractarian ranks and helped start The Guardian as the High Church organ. Shaken by Newman's secession, the Gorham judgment, and the condemnations of Pusey and Ward, he was received into the Catholic Church in 1852 after a retreat at Clapham.

Ordained in 1856, Coleridge entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1857 and in 1865 became the Jesuit editor of The Month, adding The Messenger in 1877. He projected the Quarterly Series and wrote The Public Life of Our Lord, lives of Francis Xavier and Teresa, and the gospel harmony Vita Vitae Nostrae. Failing health forced his resignation from The Month in 1881, and after a seizure in 1890 he finished his work at Roehampton before dying in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ma:
This article treats marriage chiefly as a lasting condition, with its moral and social aspects, rather than as a mere ceremony. Marriage is usually defined as the legitimate union of husband and wife. Legitimate means sanctioned by natural, evangelical, or civil law, and husband and wife implies mutual rights, life in common, and an enduring bond. Those last marks set marriage apart from concubinage and fornication.

The definition is broad enough to cover polygamous and polyandrous unions allowed by civil law. The theory of primitive promiscuity, debated by writers from 1860 to 1890, finds little support in historical times. The entry then weighs deviations from marriage. It argues that Christianity gave the world its highest ideal of unadulterated monogamy, with equality between the two parties, an influence spreading far beyond Christian lands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jerome-lamy-b: Jérôme Lamy Besange, born at Linz in 1726 and dead in 1781, taught Scripture at Salzburg for twenty-four years. His published works are an Introduction to the Old Testament in two volumes, an Introduction to the Four Gospels, an Introduction to the Acts of the Apostles. There is also a commentary on the Passion called Fasciculus Myrrhae, and a rendering of the seven penitential psalms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-lafarge:
John LaFarge was an American painter, decorator, and writer who revolutionized stained glass. Born in New York in 1835 to a French naval officer father, he studied at Mount St. Mary's and Fordham, meant to study law, but after Paris study with Couture turned to art. His early Newport landscapes already showed originality in color values and the influence of Japanese art, which he pioneered studying.

Experimenting with color, he rivaled medieval windows. He added new resources by inventing opalescent glass and methods of superimposing and welding it, seen in the Battle Window at Harvard and the Peacock Window at Worcester. His mural work began at Trinity Church, Boston, in 1873, and in his seventy-first year he painted lunettes on the history of religion for the St. Paul capitol. His books on painting, Japan, and the masters matched a wide-ranging mind.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kimberley-in-:
Kimberley in Orange is a South African vicariate, a missionary district, that grew out of the Eastern District and then the Vicariate of Natal. It became separate in 1886, covering Basutoland, Griqualand-West, Bechuanaland, and the Orange River Colony, though Basutoland split off as its own prefecture on 8 May 1894.

Before diamonds, the white settlers were almost all Boers and Catholics were few. Diamonds found about 1867 drew crowds to Kimberley from 1870, most of them Irish and English. Early priests worked in thin soil. Father Hoendervangers followed troops as a military chaplain in 1854 and built a Bloemfontein church. His successor Father Bompart served a flock of eight or ten poor Catholics, often near starvation, among neighbours hostile to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-knowledge:
Knowledge is treated here as a basic fact of awareness that cannot be strictly defined, only clarified. The article opens from everyday speech: knowing a man, knowing a fact, knowing a lesson, and knowing a science each mean something different.

Those uses fall into two kinds: sense knowledge of particular things, and understanding of general laws. Many tongues mark the split with two verbs, like Greek gnonai and eidenai or German kennen and wissen. Knowledge always joins a knowing subject to a known object, whether event, theorem, mind, or God. Three parts follow: the essentials of knowledge, its kinds, and the problem of knowledge itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liberatus-of-:
Liberatus of Carthage, a sixth-century archdeacon, wrote a history of Nestorian and Monophysite troubles. In 535 he travelled to Rome as legate of an African synod of 217 bishops, to consult Pope Agapetus I. Like most Africans he opposed Justinian's 544 edict against the Three Chapters, and African bishops often used him as ambassador in its disputes.

 He meant to show how misjudged was the Three Chapters' condemnation by the emperor. The work, A Short Account of the Nestorians and Eutychians, runs from Nestorius's ordination in 428 to Constantinople II in 553. Since he names Theodosius of Alexandria as still alive, it was written before 567, while he also records Pope Vigilius's death in June 555. His sources are Cassiodorus, synod acts, and contemporary letters. Despite his controversial purpose and anger at Monophysites and backers of the condemnation, his history is well and fairly written, an important document for the two heresies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liege:
Liege, canonical name Leodiensis, is now the capital of its Belgian province of the same name. The diocese's first capital was Tongres, northeast of Liege. Its land first belonged to Trier, then Cologne, but Tongres gained autonomy after the fourth century's first half. Its bounds, those of the Civitas Tungrorum, were unchanged until 1559. Thus Tongres stretched from Chimay to Stavelot, Aachen, Gladbach, and Venlo, taking in Latin and Germanic peoples.

 St. Servais, installed in 344 or 345, was the first bishop, present at Rimini's council in 359-360. The Franks' conversion began under Falco and went on under Domitian, Monulphus, and Gondulphus. St. Amandus (647-650) and St. Remaculus (650-660) quit the chair in discouragement and built monasteries. St. Lambert (669-705) finished the pagans' conversion and was probably murdered about 705 for defending church property. His successor St. Hubert built a basilica to house his relics, which became the city's nucleus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liguge:
Liguge is a Benedictine Abbey in Poitiers diocese, founded about 360 by St. Martin of Tours. When St. Martin became Bishop of Tours and set up Marmoutiers nearby, Liguge's fame declined. Among his successors were St. Savin, who became a hermit, and Abbot Ursinus, in whose reign Defensor compiled the Scintillarum Liber.

Saracen invasion, Aquitaine wars, and Norman invasion nearly wrecked the monastery, which by the eleventh century had fallen to a dependent priory of Maillezais, finally a benefice in commendam. The commendatory prior Geoffrey d'Estissac, friend of Rabelais, built the existing church. In 1607 Liguge passed to the Jesuit college of Poitiers. At the Revolution the buildings and lands were sold. In 1852 Bishop Pie set up a colony of monks at Liguge. When, in 1880, the monks were driven out under the Ferry laws, many retired under Dom Bourigaud to Silos in Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-henri-d:
Louis Henri de Lestrange, in religion Dom Augustine, was a Trappist abbot and founder, born in Ardeche in 1754 and dead at Lyons in 1827. Fourteenth child of a court officer, he was ordained in 1778 and made vicar-general of Vienne, with a bishopric in view.

Fleeing that prospect, he entered La Trappe in 1780. When revolution suppressed the orders in 1790, he led twenty-four monks to Val-Sainte in Switzerland, then planted houses in Spain, Piedmont, Belgium, and England. Driven out again in 1798, he scattered his monks to Poland and Podolia, regained Val-Sainte in 1802, sent a colony to America, and founded Cervara in Genoa in 1804.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manuterge:
Manuterge was the towel a priest used in liturgical service. Two kinds existed. One served the sacristy, for washing hands before Mass, before Communion outside Mass, and before baptism. It might also dry hands after customary washings after Mass. No rules fixed its material or form, and it often hung over a roller with ends sewn into a loop.

Hand washing before Mass reaches back to early Christian days and appears in ninth- and tenth-century sacramentaries. The second manuterge served at Mass itself, drying hands at the Lavabo after the Offertory, as the priest recited the Lavabo psalm, and for a bishop before the Offertory and after Communion. Kept on the credence table with finger bowl and cruets, it was usually small, about eighteen by fourteen inches, washing only thumb and two fingertips. Lace or embroidery trimmed its ends, and fifth-century ordination statutes already named it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maynooth-coll:
Maynooth College, the National College of Saint Patrick at Maynooth in County Kildare, twelve miles from Dublin, was founded in 1795. Ireland then still had its own Parliament, and though Catholics could not sit in it, the spirit of toleration from America and France seeped into its debates. During their brief parliamentary liberty from 1782 to 1801, Irish Protestants backed national brotherhood and produced Edmund Burke and Henry Grattan, to whom the college's founding is chiefly ascribed.

Other forces helped. The United Irishmen preached universal toleration. London wished to shield young Irish priests from revolutionary contagion on the Continent. Soldiers were also needed in wartime from a class that supplied Ireland's best recruits. In 1794 Dr. Troy memorialized the viceroy, and the college opened the next year. The entry follows its early years as a home-grown seminary built by a rare alliance of Protestant goodwill and government interest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mixed-marriag:
Mixed marriage, in Latin matrimonia mixta, technically means a marriage between a Catholic and a non-Catholic baptized in some Christian sect. The term is also often used for unions between Catholics and infidels. The Church has resisted such unions from its earliest days, because Christ lifted wedlock to sacramental dignity.

A Catholic wedding a non-Catholic was rightly judged to cheapen wedlock's holy nature, since it joined in sacred things with one outside the fold. St. Paul insists strongly on Christian marriage's unity of faith. The article sets out the canonical discipline. Such marriages need dispensation, the Catholic party must promise to keep the faith and raise the children Catholic, and the non-Catholic party must be informed of these promises.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moral-and-can:
Marriage, in this entry's moral and canonical treatment, is the union by which a man and a woman form one principle of generation. They do so through mutual consent, sharing life, raising children and supporting each other in lasting affection. It is a contract by nature above human law, instituted by God and subject to divine law. No human power can rescind it.

Its primary end is the begetting and raising of children of God. Mutual society and help and a lawful remedy for concupiscence are secondary ends.
