Marriage is monogamous and indissoluble, dissolved only by death once consummated. The entry then works through impediments, consent and form. It sets out how the Church judges validity and what follows when a union fails.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-st-mary:
Mount Saint Mary's College, the second oldest Catholic collegiate institution in the United States, stands near Emmitsburg, Maryland. It lies in the Archdiocese of Baltimore, on high ground at the foot of the Blue Ridge. The site is prized for beauty, health and room for exercise. Its theological seminary has run alongside the college since its foundation.

Directed by an association of secular clergy with lay professors, it is governed by a board chaired ex officio by Baltimore's archbishop. It counted sixteen professors with 298 college students and 54 seminarians in 1909-10. Founded in 1808 when the Sulpicians moved their preparatory seminary from Pigeon Hill, it began with eight students under its first president, John Dubois. It grew through four departments teaching arts, commerce and modern languages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-marr:
In Old and New Testament, God's love for man and his dealings with his chosen people are often pictured as bridegroom and bride. Christian virginity, too, has been seen from the earliest centuries as a soul's special offering to its spouse, Christ. That sense seems to lie behind talk of the mystical nuptials of Saint Agnes and Saint Catherine of Alexandria.

Later the phrase mystical marriage took two senses, one wide and one restricted. In the wide sense, found in many saints' lives, Christ appears in vision, calls a soul his bride, gives the customary ring, and the Virgin, saints and angels attend a ceremony. The rite symbolises a purely spiritual grace: a sudden growth of charity and familiarity with God, and his special care thereafter. The restricted sense marks a rarer, higher union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-hall-st-e:
Old Hall, or Saint Edmund's College, near Ware in Hertfordshire, carried Douai's work for southern England after the Revolution. Founded on 16 November 1793, Saint Edmund's feast, it began when Bishop Douglass gathered four Douai students at a house already holding a Catholic school from 1749.

A legacy of ten thousand pounds left by John Sone let Douglass build a college blessed in 1799, with chapel and refectory added in 1805. Seminary of the London district until 1850, it then passed to Westminster and Southwark, flourishing under Thomas Griffiths from 1818. Thomas Griffiths, president from 1818 to 1834, later became vicar apostolic of London.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-st-:
Orders of Saint George share only their patron, the soldier martyr of Lydda, and otherwise stand as independent bodies across countries and centuries. Byzantine art showed George as a horseman in full arms, and crusading knights, recognizing their own gear, adopted him as patron of knighthood.

From that popularity sprang secular and religious associations alike. England's Garter, still seated at Saint George's chapel, Windsor, joins the 1818 order of Saint Michael and Saint George for foreign service, with Bavarian, Russian, and other orders catalogued. Saint George, a martyr of Diocletian’s persecution in the fourth century, is the patron in question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oscott-st-mar:
Oscott, or Saint Mary's College, began in 1793 when English Catholic nobility and gentry formed a committee to school their sons and train clergy on English soil. Buildings meant for the bishop's house at Oscott, a hamlet four miles north of Birmingham, were handed to the plan. John Bew became president in February 1794, the first three boys arrived in May, and the college opened formally in November.

Early years were gloomy until Bishop Milner took the college with its debts in 1808 and revived it. Under Henry Weedall, president from 1824 to 1840, numbers outgrew the old buildings. A stately new Gothic college rose near Sutton Coldfield, and Bishop Wiseman succeeded Weedall in 1840. The entry follows presidents, buildings, and the college's growth into a leading English Catholic seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patron-and-pa:
Patronage, or ius patronatus, is a set bundle of rights and duties falling to a definite person, the patron, chiefly over assigning and running a benefice. It comes not from hierarchical rank but from the Church's lawful grant in gratitude to a benefactor. Since patronal rights touch the spiritual order, decretals call patronage a right annexed to spiritual things. It falls under church law and courts, though property questions draw civil law and courts deep into the matter.

Eastern founders could nominate a temporal administrator and suggest a cleric to the bishop. In the West, Orange in 441 gave a bishop building in another diocese the right of presentation, and Toledo in 655 gave each lay church-builder the same, without ownership. Among Germanic peoples, temple and church rights of builders and lords grew into the full medieval patronage system, whose kinds, transfer, and loss later pages sort in detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perge:
Perge was a chief city of Pamphylia, set between two rivers about sixty stadia from the sea. Its ruins still show a theatre, a wrestling ground, a temple of Artemis outside the walls, and two churches. Paul and Barnabas passed through on their first missionary journey, probably without preaching, and it was there that John Mark left them for Jerusalem. On the return from Pisidia, Paul preached at Perge.

As a church centre the city lasted long. Greek lists call it metropolis of Pamphylia Secunda into the thirteenth century. Le Quien counts eleven of its bishops, from Epidaurus at Ancyra in 312 through figures at Nicaea, Ephesus, Chalcedon, and Constantinople. Among them were a condemned Monothelite, Apergius, and an Iconoclast, Sisinnius Pastillas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-privilege:
Privilege, from Latin privilegium, like a private law, is a lasting grant made by a lawgiver outside the common law. It is given by special favour and gives the favoured an edge over the unfavoured. Since the favour lasts, it differs from a permission or a single dispensation.

It is granted by a superior with authority over the law, so it bears a weight near a law's, and others must respect its use. A privilege departs from the common law, whether it merely adds to it or cuts against it. Privileges take many kinds. Some are built into the law, clausa in corpore juris, such as clerics' privileges, while others come by special rescript. Some are added to the law, praeter jus, touching what the law leaves alone. Others stand against the law, contra jus, forming an exception that lets one do or skip what the law forbids or commands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-putative-marr:
Putative, from the Latin putativus, means supposed, reputed or commonly believed. This short encyclopedia entry applies the word to marriage in canon law. A putative marriage is an alliance commonly reputed valid, and sincerely believed by at least one party to be valid in the Church's eyes, because it was entered in good faith. In reality it is null and void, since a diriment impediment, a bar that annuls marriage, stands in its way.

The Church still treats such a marriage as standing in her external forum, her public legal order, until its invalidity is proved. Children born of it keep the rights of legitimacy. Gasparri's work on marriage and Rosset's treatise supply the entry's authorities. Readers of canon law find here a brief, exact note on how good faith softens the harsh edge of an invalid union.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ritual-of-mar:
The ritual of marriage in the Rituale Romanum of today is remarkably simple. It consists of a declaration of consent by both parties, ratified by the priest with the words Ego conjungo vos in matrimonium. Next comes a blessing of the ring. The bridegroom receives it back from the priest and places it on the ring finger of the bride's left hand. A final benedictory prayer completes the ceremony.

The rite should be followed by the Nuptial Mass. It has a blessing after the Pater Noster and a shorter blessing before the benediction. At that Mass the couple are advised to receive communion. A special rubric from the Council of Trent orders that laudable local customs beyond this form should be kept. The contracting parties themselves are the ministers of the sacrament. Its words must be spoken in the vernacular.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabbatine-pri:
The Sabbatine Privilege takes its name from the apocryphal Bull Sacratissimo uti culmine of John XXII, dated 3 March 1322. In it, the pope tells how the Mother of God appeared to him, praising the Carmelite Order. The Virgin asked John, as Christ's representative, to ratify indulgences already granted in heaven. These were a plenary indulgence for order members and a partial indulgence for confraternity members. She herself would descend on the Saturday after their death and free those in purgatory, conducting them to heaven.

Our first information of this Bull comes from the Carmelite Balduinus Leersius, who died in 1483. Its authenticity was keenly contested in the seventeenth century but vigorously defended by Carmelites. Chief opponents were Joannes Launoy and the Bollandist Daniel Papebroch. Today scholars universally regard it as inauthentic, even the Carmelite Zimmerman's Monumenta joining in rejection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrament-of-:
For Catholics it is certain that Christian marriage between baptized persons counts as a true sacrament under the New Law, strictly understood. Trent defines in canon one of session twenty-four that matrimony is truly one of the Seven Sacraments, instituted by Christ and conferring grace. Anyone denying this is anathema. The occasion was the Reformers' denial of marriage's sacramental character.

Calvin, in his Institutes, allowed matrimony was instituted by God but asked what sober man could call it a sacrament. Agriculture, architecture, and shoemaking are also God's ordinances but not sacraments. Luther called marriage an external worldly thing like clothes and food, subject to worldly authority. Trent's fathers evidently had Luther's passage in mind. But Trent was not first. Florence's Decree for the Armenians had already called matrimony the seventh sacrament, a figure of Christ and the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacrilege:
Sacrilege generally means violating or mistreating a sacred object. Loosely, any offence against religion counts as sacrilege. Theologians agree that only what has been dedicated to God's worship by a public rite counts as sacred. Public authority must intervene; private initiative does not suffice. Giving a thing sacred character is a juridical act of the Church.

Three kinds are enumerated: personal, local, and real. St Thomas teaches that a different holiness attaches to persons, places, and things. Suarez accepts the division as agreeing with the canons. Personal sacrilege means dealing so irreverently with a sacred person that honour due is breached. It is committed chiefly in three ways. Laying violent hands on a cleric, violating ecclesiastical immunity, and sins against chastity by the consecrated are its chief forms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-eugeniu:
Eugenius was unanimously elected Bishop of Carthage in 480 and died 13 July 505. The election was deferred by Arian opposition. The bishop's wise government, charity, austerity, and courage under persecution won even Arians' admiration. In defence of the Word's Divinity he was imitated by his flock. Many were exiled with him after he admitted Vandals against royal edict.

Both sides claimed the name Catholic. The conference ended when the chief Arian bishop withdrew, pleading he could not speak Latin. Enraged, Huneric exiled bishops to Corsica and African deserts. Among the latter was Eugenius, who dwelt in Tripoli's desert. Setting out, he wrote a consolation letter to Carthage's faithful. Gunthamund allowed Eugenius to return. After eight years' peace Thrasamund exiled Eugenius to Vienne. There Eugenius built a monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-selge:
Selge, a titular see in Pamphylia Prima suffragan to Side, stood in a fertile plain on the south slope of the Taurus mountains. It boasted a founding by the seer Calchas, but it was probably a Spartan colony in truth. Hard to reach, it still grew into the most populous and powerful city of Pisidia. Its army of 2,000 soldiers stayed in constant strife with neighboring cities.

Selge sought Alexander's friendship as he passed through Pisidia. In 208 BC it was besieged by Achaeus and forced to pay a heavy war tax. Its coins show it flourishing under Trajan. By the fifth century it was only a small city, yet still able to beat off a Gothic attack. Four bishops are named, and ruins of temples, an aqueduct, a stadium, and a theatre remain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ou:
Jean Eudes founded the Institute of Our Lady of Charity at Caen, Normandy, in 1641, under the title of Our Lady of Refuge. Out of compassion for women abandoned to a life of sin, Eudes first gathered penitents under good and zealous women. A house opened at Rennes, and the institute spread until seven communities stood in France when the Revolution broke out.

The Order of the Good Shepherd sprang from this parent institute. The sisters do not limit their work to reclaiming the fallen; they also receive girls in danger of being lost or brought up immorally, forming a class of preservation. Government reformatories attach to some monasteries. Each house keeps its own novitiate and independence, while the mother-house remains at Caen.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-for-p:
Founded on 8 March 1698 by four laymen and the clergyman Thomas Bray, the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge is the greatest society within the Church of England. Bray, the Bishop of London's commissary in Maryland, drove the plan to consult together to promote Christian knowledge. Backed by bishops including Gilbert Burnet of Salisbury, the society first aimed at educating poor children, founding six London schools within two years and nearly 2,000 charity schools by 1741.

Later the society turned to training teachers, maintaining Saint Katharine's College, Tottenham, and supporting diocesan training colleges. Its schools work passed to a new National Society and, after 1870, to the State. As the Church of England's great publishing house it printed cheap books, tracts, and pictures, circulating over 11 million publications besides Bibles, prayer books, and tracts in 1905. It also ran evening schools, prison instruction, hospital visits, medical missions, emigrant aid, and a training college for lay workers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-carthage:
St. Carthage — Mochuda is another form of his name — was born about 555 to a good family in what is now County Kerry, Ireland. This entry follows a youth who herded swine near Castlemaine, then became a monk in a neighbouring monastery under St. Carthage the Elder, later receiving priest's orders. In 580 he resolved on a hermit's life, building a cell at Kiltallagh, where pilgrims soon flocked to his fame.

After a few years, two neighbouring bishops, jealous of him, forced him to quit his hermitage, and he went on a visit to Bangor, where he spent a year. On St. Comgall's advice he went back to Kerry, founding churches at Kilcarragh and Kilfeighney. He then visited Waterford, Clonfert-molua, and Lynally, whence, on St. Colman Elo's recommendation, he settled at Rahan near Tullamore. There he founded his monastery of Rahan about 590.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-cyprian-of:
St. Cyprian of Carthage, Thaschus Caecilius Cyprianus, was bishop and martyr. This entry follows a man whose birth date and early life are unknown. By his conversion to Christianity he had, perhaps, passed middle life. A famous orator and pleader, he had considerable wealth and undoubtedly held a great position in Africa's metropolis.

His deacon, St. Pontius, whose life of the saint survives, tells us his manner was dignified without severity, cheerful without effusiveness. His writings show his gift of eloquence. He was no thinker, philosopher, or theologian, but a man of the world through and through, an administrator of vast energies and forcible, striking character. Caecilianus, an aged priest he seems to have lived with, brought about his conversion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elphege:
Elphege, martyred archbishop of Canterbury, died at his captors' hands because no ransom would be paid for him. Born in 954, he left his widowed mother and inheritance for Deerhurst monastery, lived as an anchorite at Bath, became its abbot, then bishop of Winchester in 984. In 1006 he became archbishop and travelled to Rome for the pallium. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his murder at Greenwich to 19 April 1012.

Danes sacked Canterbury in September 1011 and carried him prisoner. Drunk and enraged at the refused ransom, they pelted him with ox bones and stones until one Thurm finished him with an axe. Canute later moved his body to Canterbury, where his principal feast falls on 19 April. Earlier, Elphege had confirmed Olaf of Norway at Andover in 994.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-george:
George, martyr and patron of England, is among the most famous saints about whom the least can be safely said. Delehaye's careful investigation sums the firm record in one line: he suffered at or near Lydda, Diospolis, in Palestine, probably before Constantine. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 insists his historical existence is not in doubt, despite absence from Syrian and primitive Hieronymian martyrologies.

The earliest known narrative, surviving partly in a fifth-century palimpsest, is full of incredible marvels: three deaths by chopping, burial, and fire, each undone by God's power. Gelasius's decree of 495 already counted his Acts apocryphal, revering his name while leaving his deeds to God alone. Nor was he the martyr who tore down Diocletian's edict, nor Gibbon's Arian bishop in disguise. The entry leaves a name, a shrine, and a legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-john-tweng:
John Twenge, prior of Bridlington, is the last English saint canonized, a canon regular famed for miracles. Born near Bridlington in 1319 to the Yorkshire Twenge family, which later gave two priest-martyrs and helped found York's Bar Convent Institute, he studied at Oxford, then entered Bridlington Priory. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Bridlington to 1379.

Charged successively with community offices, he was finally, despite reluctance, elected prior, holding office until death. Even in life he enjoyed a reputation for holiness and miraculous power. Once he changed water into wine. Once five Hartlepool seamen, fearing shipwreck, called on God in his servant John's name, and the prior himself appeared in canonical habit, bringing them safely to shore. After death, miracles by his intercession spread rapidly, and Archbishop Neville ordered evidence gathered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-juliana-of:
Juliana of Liège, nun of Mont-Cornillon, spent her energies winning the feast of Corpus Christi for the Church. Born at Retinnes near Liège in 1193, she lost her parents at five and entered Mont-Cornillon convent. She progressed rapidly, reading Augustine and Bernard with pleasure, and loved Mary, the Passion, and above all the Blessed Sacrament. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Fosses to 5 April 1258.

She took the veil in 1206 and served the sick in the hospital there. Early she bent every energy to introducing Corpus Christi's feast. Chosen superioress unanimously in 1230, she soon faced heavy trials. The convent's general superior Roger had bought his post by intrigue and bribery in 1233. A vicious, scandalous man, he hated her virtue and reproaches, and stirred the populace against her. She fled to Eve of Liège's cell, then to a canon's house, and was vindicated in time.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stonyhurst-co:
Stonyhurst College in Lancashire descends from a school founded at St Omer in 1592. It served English boys barred from Catholic schooling at home. This entry follows the college through exile after exile, driven from St Omer in 1762, sheltered at Bruges, then dispersed when the Jesuits were suppressed in 1773.

Staff and pupils regrouped at Liège, then settled at Stonyhurst Hall in 1794. The curriculum first followed Jesuit classical ideals, then opened to modern languages, science, and public exams. Observatory, library, masters, alumni, and the school magazine all appear here. Together they picture a school whose roots run back more than three hundred years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-scots-col:
Scotland's college at Rome, gift of Clement VIII, is traced here from bull to buildings. The foundation bull of 5 December 1600 granted all privileges already enjoyed by Greek, German, and English colleges. Endowments followed, including an abbey's revenue in the Neapolitan kingdom and a monthly pension from the Dataria. The old Scotch Hospice's revenues joined later.

First students arrived in 1602 and lodged two years in the Via Tritone before moving in 1604 to Via Quattro Fontane, near the Quirinal Palace. Modest first buildings gave way, about half a century before 1913, to Poletti's handsome and commodious college, admired for graceful architecture. Rectors, students, and Scottish mission links complete the story.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trinity-colle:
A college for Catholic women in Washington, D.C., chartered in 1897 with power to confer degrees. It grew from the Sisters of Notre Dame de Namur's wish for a select day-school at Brookland. At the Catholic University's suggestion it became a college matching the women's colleges already founded in the United States.

Cardinal Gibbons, the university's chancellor, warmly backed the plan, and Sister Julia, provincial superior, secured thirty-three acres between Michigan and Lincoln Avenues. The corner-stone was laid on 8 December 1899, and South Hall was dedicated in November 1900. The finished building holds residence halls for two hundred students and a library of 12,000 volumes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
Cambridge's origins lie in obscurity, and no certain date can be fixed for the foundation of the great seat of learning now known as the university. In Elizabeth's day wild legends circulated, with Oxford claiming Greek professors who came with Brutus of Troy. Cambridge traced itself to Cantaber, a Spanish prince said to have reached Britain in the year of the world 3588. The chronicler Peter de Blois, assigning learned monks to Cambridge in 1110, is no more trustworthy.

The entry sifts these fables and follows the real growth of schools, colleges, and faculties from the twelfth century onward. It covers the coming of the religious orders, the founding of colleges, the struggles with town and crown, and the later reforms that shaped the modern university. Readers get both a debunking of antiquarian myth and a solid outline of Cambridge's rise.

St Francis Xavier's at Antigonish, Nova Scotia, was founded in 1885 as St Francis Xavier's College by Bishop MacKinnon of Arichat, now the Diocese of Antigonish. A legislative act of 1866 had empowered it to confer degrees, and a statute of 1882 granted full university powers. The new charter of 1909 gave it all the powers any university could reasonably ask of the state. That included the right to confer every usual degree and to hold property of any value.

The supreme governing body is a board of twelve governors, with the Bishop of Antigonish as chairman by office. In 1912 the college counted twenty-five professors, lecturers, and tutors, and in 1911 and 1912 it counted 356 students, mostly from the Maritime Provinces. The entry sketches a young Catholic college serving Scottish and Acadian communities on Canada's Atlantic edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ushaw-college:
Ushaw College, or the College of St Cuthbert, is a combined college and seminary for the six dioceses once comprised in England's old Northern Vicariate. Its government rests in a united board of those dioceses' bishops, with a president, a vice-president, and about thirty professors. Students average over 300, split into three courses: a preparatory course of about eighty boys, a humanity course of about 130, and a philosophical and theological course of about 100.

Its history begins with the suppression of the English college at Douai, which for 200 years had embodied the Catholic faith for England, one of the French Revolution's many far-reaching results. English Catholics urgently needed a home successor to continue Douai's work. The entry follows the college's founding at Ushaw, its buildings, and its staff, giving the story of a seminary born from exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-validation-of:
Validation of marriage repairs a union that is null, and this entry sets out the canon law of the cure. When nullity comes only from defective consent in one or both parties, a simple renewal of consent suffices. When some church impediment makes the marriage invalid, it may be healed by simple dispensation or by sanatio in radice, healing at the root.

In the first method, once a dispensation from the impediment is granted, a fresh consent of both parties validates the marriage. If the impediment touched only one party and the other knew nothing of it, both probably must still renew consent. True renewal requires the parties to know of the nullity, unless sanatio in radice is used. The entry works through the cases with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ann:
Anne de Xainctonge was the Dijon-born foundress of the Sisters of St Ursula of the Blessed Virgin. Born in 1567 to a councillor of the Dijon parliament, she watched the Jesuit college from her family's house and conceived a new idea: religious women who were not cloistered. Running public schools where girls would be educated, not sold an education.

Against the prejudices of her time and her parents' opposition, and guided by Jesuit directors, she opened her first convent at Dôle in Franche-Comté on 16 June 1606, with two companions. The company took Our Lady as general and St Ursula as lieutenant, with the Rule of St Ignatius as its pattern. For fifteen years she founded new houses across eastern France and Switzerland. Her beatification cause was later wrecked when wars and the Revolution destroyed its documents, then re-established.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ant:
Anthony Page was an English martyr executed at York in April 1593. Born at Harrow-on-the-Hill in 1571, of gentle birth, he entered Christ Church, Oxford, in 1581, then the English College at Reims in 1584. He was ordained deacon at Laon in 1590 and priest at Reims in 1591.

His contemporary Anthony Champney described him as wonderfully meek, modest, and pure, of more than common learning and piety, endearing himself to all by candour of mind and sweetness of behaviour. Condemned for being a priest under the statute of 27 Elizabeth, he was hanged, disembowelled, and quartered. The entry gives his death date uncertainly, as 20 or 30 April 1593.
childe-harold-s-pilgrimage:
Lord Byron's Childe Harold's Pilgrimage is a long poem in four cantos, addressed first to Ianthe. A dedication in verse praises the young girl's guileless heart before Harold appears. The pilgrim himself is a satiated young lord who leaves England to wander. Spain and Portugal, fresh from Peninsular war, fill the first canto.

Greece under Turkish rule fills the second, with lament for her fallen glory. The third canto crosses Waterloo's field to Switzerland, Byron's own exile written into Harold's. The fourth wanders Italy: Venice, Florence, and Rome in decay. Byron published the cantos over six years and woke famous after the first. Harold's gloom became the Byronic hero, copied across Europe. The poem mixes travel description, history, and confession in Spenserian stanzas of sustained splendour, and it made modern tourism melancholy.
cicero-de-natura-deorum-yonge:
Cicero's On the Nature of the Gods, written in 45 BC, stages a debate on religion among Rome's educated elite. C. D. Yonge's translation, from the Harper edition of 1877, is the text here. Cicero sets the scene at a friend's villa and mostly listens.

An Epicurean speaker argues the gods exist but care nothing for human affairs. A Stoic answers that divine reason runs the world and watches over it. An Academic skeptic then takes both cases apart, finding each one wanting. The dialogue is the fullest surviving survey of ancient thought on the gods, and its balance made it a school text for centuries.
cicero-philippics-yonge:
Cicero's Philippics are fourteen speeches against Mark Antony, delivered in 44 and 43 BC after the murder of Julius Caesar. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here, drawn from the fourth volume of his Orations. Cicero named them after Demosthenes' speeches against Philip of Macedon.

An old man with no army, Cicero used speech alone to brand Antony a public enemy and rally the Senate against him. The gamble worked for a season, then failed: the triumvirs proscribed him, and Antony had him killed in December 43 BC. The speeches are his last stand for the republic. They cost him his life and fixed his fame.
cicero-tusculan-disputations-yonge:
Cicero wrote the Tusculan Disputations in 45 BC at his villa in Tusculum, in the last stretch of his career. C. D. Yonge's English translation is the text here. The work holds five days of talk with friends on how to face life's hardest blows.

Each day takes one fear: death, pain, grief, the passions of the soul, and the question whether virtue alone makes a happy life. Cicero argues death is no evil, pain can be borne, and grief yields to reason. His answers lean Stoic, though he keeps his Academic freedom to doubt. The talks became a handbook of calm for later ages.
diary-of-a-pilgrimage:
Jerome K Jerome's Diary of a Pilgrimage, first published in April 1891 and reprinted steadily for decades, sends Jerome and his friend B to Germany for the Oberammergau Passion Play. The title page lists him as author of Three Men in a Boat, and the comedy runs on the same rails: packing, trains, and German hotels. A friend's patent tea-basket, complete from caddy to methylated spirit stove, opens the preparations.

At Oberammergau the jokes quieten before the play's sincerity, and Jerome writes about it with unexpected respect. Along the way he complains of phrasebooks full of raspberries, figs, and medlars no traveler ever wants. The diary mixes farce and genuine feeling in the proportion that made Jerome beloved.

english-men-of-letters-coleridge:
H. D. Traill's Coleridge, from the English Men of Letters series, attempts a short life and critical estimate of Samuel Taylor Coleridge. Traill quotes De Quincey's warning that Coleridge's multiform attainments make enormous demands on any biographer, and he admits the shortcomings his narrow limits impose.

No complete biography of Coleridge on an important scale then existed, Traill notes, and no critical appreciation had yet correlated the whole work with the changes of his life. His volume tries to do both in brief: the poet, philosopher and talker, and the circumstances that shaped him. Readers meeting Coleridge for the first time will find Traill a sane, readable guide to a famously difficult man.
faxian-record-buddhistic-kingdoms-legge:
Faxian, a Chinese Buddhist monk, recorded his pilgrimage to India in 414 CE. James Legge translated the Record of Buddhistic Kingdoms into English. Faxian had walked from China through Central Asia between 399 and 414.

He crossed deserts and mountains seeking complete texts of monastic rules. Kingdoms, monasteries, and relics of the Buddha fill his spare narrative. Storms at sea nearly ended his return voyage with his books. The record is the earliest surviving Chinese travel narrative of its kind. Legge's translation trails him past countries now transformed or gone. Adventure and devotion combine in Faxian's calm, factual voice throughout.
framley-parsonage:
Anthony Trollope continues the Barsetshire chronicles in this novel of the vicar of Framley. Mark Robarts holds the living of Framley through the patronage of Lady Lufton, whose son Lord Lufton is his closest friend. The contents open with the two sets of the county, the Framley set and the Chaldicotes set, between which the young clergyman must steer.

Robarts is flattered into the faster company of Mr. Sowerby and signs bills he cannot pay. Debt pulls him toward disgrace while his wife Fanny holds the household together. Lady Lufton's opposition to her son's marriage to Lucy Robarts, the vicar's sister, runs as the second thread. Trollope lets money, patronage, and clerical pride do the damage, and rescue comes slowly and at a price.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BernauGeorgePro: Gary Hart, the Colorado senator with a lifelong interest in the Kennedy era, is the reviewer in this file: his subject is 'Promises to Keep' by George Bernau. The document preserves the review as released, a senator's published judgment on a book from the Kennedy literature that fills this archive. It is kept as issued, one of the many press pieces gathered by the researchers who collected everything the case produced in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ColumbiaCollege:
In April 1970 Harold Weisberg quarreled by mail with Mirron Alexandroff, president of Columbia College in Chicago. The subject was Sherman Skolnick, the Chicago researcher, whom Weisberg accused of plagiarizing his materials in a federal court filing.

Skolnick taught and broadcast in Chicago and drew on the case's literature freely, and Weisberg guarded his documents with famous jealousy. The letters show the movement's internal policing: credit and theft argued out, with a college president drawn into the exchange. It sits in Weisberg's files as an unusually formal record of a researchers' feud, argued on letterheads.
